title: The Odds on Alphabet's $200B AI Build
dek: Alphabet beat on revenue, on Cloud and on margin, then fell about 5% because capex went up. The market is sorting hyperscalers by how much they spend. The variable that decides whether a build pays off is how much of it was sold before it was poured.
summary: Alphabet reported Q2 2026 on July 22 with revenue +24% to $119.8B, Google Cloud +82% to $24.8B, Cloud operating margin tripled year-over-year to 35.6% and contracted backlog at $514B — and the stock fell about 5%, because full-year capex guidance rose to $195–205B and free cash flow turned negative at −$5.9B. The market is now sorting the hyperscalers by how much they spend. Read across the seven names in our coverage that are building AI infrastructure, spend size predicts almost nothing. What predicts a payoff is how much of the build is contracted before it is poured, who absorbs the loss if those contracts do not convert, and whether the builder owns the silicon that sets its own cost floor. On that test Alphabet cleared three of four gates in the same quarter it was de-rated, and the gate still open — free cash flow inflection — resolves on a 2027 schedule rather than on the size of the guide.

falsifiableBy.claim: Google Cloud's contracted backlog failing to grow beyond $514B for two consecutive quarters while capex holds at the $195–205B pace, or Cloud operating margin falling back below 25% as record-capex depreciation lands in the P&L — either would show capacity being built ahead of contracts rather than against them. A third trip: free cash flow still negative on a full-year basis when 2027 closes.

blocks.body: For three years the market paid hyperscalers to spend. Announce a datacenter, get a multiple. Some time in the first half of 2026 that reversed, and capital expenditure stopped reading as ambition and started reading as risk. Alphabet's Q2, reported July 22, is the cleanest illustration of the new regime: total revenue rose 24% to $119.8B against a roughly $117B consensus, Google Cloud grew 82% year-over-year to $24.8B, Cloud operating margin more than tripled to 35.6%, and contracted backlog reached $514B. The stock fell about 5%. The reason was one line — full-year 2026 capex guidance raised to $195–205B from $180–190B, with 2027 to rise "significantly", which pushed quarterly capex to a record $44.9B and quarterly free cash flow to −$5.9B.

**The market priced the size of the spend in the same quarter Alphabet produced the cohort's best evidence that spend converts.** That is the gap this piece is about. Nobody can hand you a probability on a $200B infrastructure program, and an article that pretends otherwise is selling a number it made up. What you can do is decompose the question into the conditions that would have to hold, check which ones have already cleared, and date the ones that have not. On Alphabet's Q2, three of four have cleared and the fourth is on a schedule.

blocks.body: The load-bearing pairing is rows two and three. If this capex were speculative — capacity poured against a demand curve someone drew on a whiteboard — you would see backlog flatten or shrink while capex climbed, and you would see margin on the already-built base compress as depreciation arrived ahead of revenue. Both moved the other way. Backlog grew $54B in a single quarter, and the margin on capacity built one and two years ago tripled year-over-year while growth *accelerated*. Negative free cash flow, in that context, is the arithmetic of building ahead of contracts you already hold. It is not evidence that the contracts are missing.

blocks.title: The underwriting test
blocks.body: Ask four questions of any AI build, in this order. **One:** how much of it is contracted before it is poured? **Two:** who absorbs the loss if those contracts do not convert — an existing cash engine, a lender, or the shareholder? **Three:** does the builder own the silicon that sets its cost floor, or is it renting someone else's margin? **Four:** is there a prior vintage of the same spend already converting at a margin you can see? None of those questions is answered by the size of the capex line, which is the only variable the July sell-off traded on.

blocks.text: Capex size is the wrong variable

blocks.body: If the size of the spend were the risk factor, the sorting would be simple: the biggest spenders carry the most danger, and the smaller programs are safer. Our coverage contains a natural control group for exactly that comparison — four companies selling the capacity to third parties under contract, one building it for its own product, and two borrowing to build it for other people. It does not sort by size, and it does not sort by tier either.

blocks.body: The three groups do not separate on spend, so put the spend next to what underwrites it. The ratio below — contracted backlog divided by the annual capex guide — is the crudest possible measure of whether a company is building against demand it already has. It is also the first cut that makes the cohort legible.

blocks.body: Read the ratio column alone and you would conclude that Oracle has the safest build in the cohort and that CoreWeave's is safer than Alphabet's. That conclusion is wrong, and the reason it is wrong is the whole argument: **contract coverage tells you the demand was booked, not that it will be honoured, and not who eats the asset if it isn't.** Oracle's ratio is a function of a $638B RPO sitting on the narrowest revenue base of the four sellers, financed through a negative-free-cash-flow window. CoreWeave's $99.4B backlog was 67% Microsoft by FY2025 revenue — a counterparty that is simultaneously spending ~$190B building the same capacity in-house. Nebius's roughly $50B is mostly two names, Meta and Microsoft, both of whom are also their own suppliers. A backlog owed to your competitor's spare capacity decision is not the same asset as a backlog owed to eight thousand enterprises.

So go one layer down, to the pillars that determine whether infrastructure revenue is durable once the contract is signed. This is where the cohort finally sorts, and it sorts nothing like the capex table.

blocks.caption: Five pillars that decide whether contracted infrastructure revenue survives renewal. Statuses are read live from each stock's analysis, so this matrix updates whenever a name is reviewed.

groups.label: Borrows to build it for others

blocks.body: The grid does two things the capex table could not. First, it collapses the neoclouds: across all five pillars CoreWeave and Nebius reach strong on none, and are rated destroyed on most — which is the framework saying, without sentiment, that renting someone else's chips against borrowed money is not a moat, however large the backlog attached to it. Their coverage ratios sit between Alphabet's and Microsoft's. Their durability does not sit anywhere near them. Second, it shows why Meta's captive build is a different instrument entirely rather than a worse one: its proprietary-data, bundling and network-effects pillars are strong, but there is no contracted third-party revenue for those pillars to defend, so the return has to arrive indirectly, through ad pricing and engagement, and cannot be underwritten in advance at all.

blocks.text: Alphabet's build has two customers and its own cost floor

blocks.body: Among the four sellers, the sorting is tighter and the honest reading is that Microsoft and Amazon carry the broadest pillar sets in the cohort. What distinguishes Alphabet's position is not moat breadth. It is four structural features of *this specific build*, all of which were visible in the quarter the market marked the stock down.

items: **Coverage that is growing faster than the spend.** Backlog went from $460B to $514B in one quarter — roughly $54B of new contracted revenue against $44.9B of capex actually spent. The build is being pre-sold at a rate slightly above the rate it is being poured, which is the only version of this cycle that does not end in stranded assets.

**A prior vintage that is visibly converting.** Cloud operating margin more than tripled year-over-year to 35.6% while revenue growth accelerated to +82%. Margin expanding *through* a record-depreciation quarter is the strongest single piece of evidence in the cohort that the capex of two years ago earns its cost of capital. Nobody else in the group produced that combination this quarter.

**Owned silicon, and now externalised capital.** TPUs mean Alphabet sets its own cost floor per unit of inference rather than paying a merchant-silicon margin on every rack — the structural advantage the neoclouds definitionally cannot have. The ~$25B TPU cloud joint venture with Blackstone formed in May 2026, targeting 500MW by 2027, extends TPU distribution beyond Alphabet's own datacenters while moving part of the capital off Alphabet's own balance sheet.

**Two customers for the same capacity.** This is the feature with no analogue elsewhere in the cohort. If external cloud demand softened, the same racks absorb Search's AI Mode inference, YouTube recommendation, and consumer Gemini — AI Mode alone is past 1B monthly users, driving queries three times longer than traditional search. Unsold capacity at CoreWeave is a stranded asset with a loan against it. Unsold capacity at Alphabet is next quarter's Search infrastructure.

blocks.body: Put together, those four are why the free-cash-flow line reads differently here than the market treated it. **A negative free cash flow quarter is information about timing, not about return, when contracted coverage is growing faster than the spend and the previous vintage is already expanding margin.** The number that would vindicate the bears is not a quarter of negative free cash flow. It is a backlog that stops growing.

blocks.text: Three places the bear is right

blocks.body: The argument above is about capital, and it is deliberately silent on the thing Alphabet's capex cannot buy. **The company's own analysis holds its talent-scarcity pillar at intact rather than strong, and the reason is model quality.** The Gemini 3.6 Flash release on July 21, 2026 landed flat on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — no shipped intelligence gain over its predecessor — leaving Alphabet's best publicly available model behind frontier releases from Anthropic and OpenAI, and beaten by cheaper, older rivals on several benchmarks. It improved efficiency and some agentic scores; it did not close the gap. Capex buys capacity. It does not buy the frontier. If enterprise AI spend routes to whoever holds the best model rather than to whoever holds the cheapest reliable capacity, the $514B backlog converts more slowly than its headline implies and Vertex is the line where you would see it first. A strong Gemini 4 reverses this; nothing else does.

The second concession is that the coverage ratios in the table above are not clean. Some share of the demand underwriting every hyperscaler commitment in this cohort is circular — model labs capitalised by hyperscalers who then contract to buy that hyperscaler's compute. Amazon's $33B into Anthropic against Anthropic's $100B+ AWS commitment is the most explicit case, Microsoft's OpenAI-heavy RPO the largest, and Alphabet holds an Anthropic minority position of its own. None of these companies disclose enough to strip the circularity out of a backlog figure. Treat every ratio in that column as an upper bound, Alphabet's included.

The third is regulatory, and it is the one risk in this piece that has nothing to do with capital allocation. Two rulings remain live as of July 2026: the DOJ and 35 states' appeal of the September 2025 search remedies, headed to the DC Circuit with oral arguments expected late 2026 or 2027, which could mandate search data-sharing and compress the CPC premium; and Judge Brinkema's ad-tech remedies decision, still pending, which could force an AdX or DFP divestiture. Search cash is what funds the build. An adverse outcome on either does not make the capex worse — it makes the funding source smaller, which is the same problem arriving by a different door.

blocks.text: Four gates, three cleared, one on a 2027 schedule

blocks.body: There is no honest single probability to quote here, so state the question as the conditions that have to hold and mark each one against the July print.

items: **Is the capacity pre-sold?** Cleared. $514B contracted, up $54B in the quarter, growing faster than the quarter's $44.9B of spend. Re-check every print: this is the number that carries the thesis.

**Does an earlier vintage already convert at a margin?** Cleared. Cloud operating margin 35.6%, more than tripled year-over-year, achieved while revenue accelerated to +82% and depreciation from the current build was already landing.
**Is the cost floor owned?** Cleared. TPU silicon plus the ~$25B Blackstone joint venture, which both externalises capital and extends TPU distribution beyond Alphabet's own footprint.

**Does free cash flow inflect on schedule?** Open, and the only one that is. Q2 was −$5.9B, 2026 guidance is $195–205B and 2027 is guided higher again, which means the trough is a 2026–27 event and the inflection is a 2027 observation. This gate cannot be argued, only waited for.

blocks.body: That distribution — three structural conditions satisfied, one timing condition outstanding — is what the framework can actually say about the odds, and it is a materially different statement from the one the tape made on July 22. The market re-priced Alphabet on gate four while gates one through three were being cleared in the same release. Whether the current price adequately compensates for the open gate is the question the [analysis page](/stocks/google) answers, live, against the scenario band; the scorecard above carries the current read.

blocks.title: What would break this
blocks.body: In order of importance. **One:** Cloud backlog stalling at or below $514B for two consecutive quarters while capex holds at the $195–205B pace — capacity being built ahead of contracts, which is the only pattern that vindicates the sell-off. **Two:** Cloud operating margin retreating below 25% as record-capex depreciation lands, which would break the claim that earlier vintages convert. **Three:** free cash flow still negative on a full-year basis when 2027 closes, pushing the payback beyond the horizon any current multiple can support. **Four:** an adverse DC Circuit or Brinkema outcome shrinking the Search cash flow that funds the whole program. A flat Gemini 4 is a fifth risk, but it caps the upside case rather than breaking the base one.

The generalisable point outlives this quarter and this company. When a category re-prices on a single visible variable — capex in 2026, per-seat billing six months ago — the framework's job is to ask whether that variable actually predicts the outcome it is being used to predict. **Spend size does not predict payoff; contracted coverage, loss absorption, cost-floor ownership and prior-vintage conversion do.** On this cohort, the capex line told you almost nothing. The four gates told you most of what is knowable, and they told you which of the seven builds is levered, which is captive, and which is being sold before it is poured.
